name: chisel
one_line: fast TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP (for pivoting)
plain: `chisel` makes a tunnel through a firewall: a server listens on one machine and a client on another connects to it over plain HTTP, then forwards ports through that single connection. In a lab this is the usual way to reach an internal network from a machine you have already compromised (a pivot).

Think of it as one outbound connection that carries many ports. The most common pattern: your Kali machine runs the server, the compromised box runs the client and offers its inside network as a SOCKS proxy that you use with proxychains.
when: Reach a service that listens only on localhost of a compromised host.
Browse or scan an internal network through a foothold.
Get through a firewall that only allows outbound web traffic.
Forward a port in either direction.

examples.title: Server on your machine
examples.explain: Listen on port 8000 and allow clients to open ports on YOUR machine (--reverse).

examples.title: Client on the target: SOCKS proxy
examples.explain: R:socks opens a SOCKS5 proxy on your machine (port 1080 by default) that exits from the target's network.

examples.title: Use the proxy
examples.explain: proxychains sends the scan through the SOCKS tunnel. Use TCP connect scans (-sT): SYN and ping scans do not work through SOCKS.

examples.title: Forward one port back to you
examples.explain: Opens port 8080 on your machine that leads to port 80 on the target's own localhost.

examples.title: Forward one port the other way
examples.explain: Without R, the client opens a local port 9000 that leads, through the server, to 10.10.10.9:3389.

examples.title: Password-protect the server
examples.explain: Stops anyone else on the network from using your tunnel. Give the client --auth user:S3cret.

examples.title: Check connectivity
examples.explain: -v prints what the client is doing: useful when it will not connect.

options.plain: Server: allow clients to ask for remote (reverse) port forwards.

Client: how many times to retry.
Remote forward: listen on the SERVER side and send to HOST:PORT from the client side.
Local forward: listen on the CLIENT side and send to HOST:PORT from the server side.
options.use: Reaching a service behind the server.

options.plain: SOCKS5 proxy on the server side (reverse) or client side (forward).

options.use: Check which build is on the target.

mistakes: Forgetting --reverse on the server when the client uses an R: remote.
Building the client for the wrong operating system or architecture (it is a single static binary: download the right one).
Using SYN scans or ping through a SOCKS proxy: use -sT -Pn.
Leaving a tunnel open without --auth on a shared network.
try: In two VMs, run the server on one and a client on the other and forward a web server's port.
Open an R:socks tunnel and scan a lab subnet with proxychains.
Time the difference between a local forward and a SOCKS pivot.
